children.text: This is why for open-weights models at least harness aware post-training is becoming a thing. Also closed source harnesses that aren't fully editable are basically an anti-pattern. The labs should just hurry up and productionize self-evolving harnesses, and have the models internalize harness engineering, so they can optimise the harness for the given task. These are solvable problems.

Hi HN, I’m Guanlan, founder of Runta. The eval runs on our runtime, so weigh this accordingly.

The short version: when you change the model, think about changing the harness too. On any one model, cost per pass varies by up to 4.4x

What we ran: 22 harness configurations × 5 open-weight models × 62 terminal tasks × 4 attempts. 27,280 runs, 83B tokens. Each harness ran with default settings at maximum reasoning effort, each trial in a fresh sandbox. Costs are Baseten list prices times reported tokens.

What we found: The lowest-cost harness changes with the model. Codex CLI ranks 1st on cost with GLM-5.3 and 15th with Kimi-K3. Paying more doesn’t buy passes. The harness with the highest pass rate ranked anywhere from 4th to 19th on cost. The model still sets most of the bill (93% of cost variation). The harness is the second lever. Starting prompt size doesn’t predict cost. Output tokens do. 64% of inference spend went to runs that didn’t pass.

children.author: Majromax
children.text:
Saying that 'steps per pass' explains cost seems nearly tautological. Run costs are proportional to the number of tokens produced, and the number of tokens is strongly correlated to the number of steps.

The 'steps per pass' criterion is also not something under the harness's direct control in the way that its tool collection and system prompt (/start tokens) are. Even the cache hit rate is hard to control beyond a limit, since modern harnesses rarely rewrite history.

I'm also suspicious about the run-to-run variance between models. Given the high variability within the presented results and the observation that failed runs (which can spin for a long time before delivering a wrong answer) account for a majority of the cost, I'm not sure that many of the conclusions here would hold up under a second sample.

A shift is realizing that refactors go from something that was costly and infrequent to something that can happen inexpensively and frequently. It takes some rebalancing.

I recently used agentic processes to bring a young codebase to a functioning state very rapidly. This forced discussions about design principles that were folded back into a short document in the repo which then led to a major refactoring plan, and a massive pruning of code that was written the week prior. There are solid engineering approaches in the codebase now that wouldn’t have been achieved without this discovery process.

Not every problem should (or even could sometimes) be solved the same way. Are you planning to maintain the produced code for more than a year? No, then wave away. But if you're expecting others to depend on it, and you want to be able to continue evolving what it is, then a tight leash and full understanding of how it actually works, is very much needed, even if you don't actually type characters into an editor anymore.

Otherwise you still end up with balls of spaghetti where each change takes longer and longer to work into the codebase. With a bit of planning, you can keep tackling changes and they keep taking the same amount of time more or less.

children.author: dcss_gardener
children.text:
You can steer it a lot with implicit context too, like ants following pheromones. If you put an empty docs/ dir in your repo agents will put documentation there without being told. If you put one inline test, they'll write every test inline. If you seed a decision record they'll record their decisions. If you have a lowercase sql query they'll use lowercase sql. If you write a test for wcag AA contrast they'll make ui with wcag AA contrast. And so on.

With some up front care you can create an environment where they mostly do what you want when you let them rip without oversight. As the codebase grows it becomes less likely they'll see any one example, and more rarely expressed ones can get missed. And then codebase predating LLMs or designed without this consideration you just have to accept what you get or wrangle them manually.

I think Conway's law applies. In an ideal situation your code mimics your organisational structure.

The places where you let an agent do its thing is bound by the (implicit) interface your prompt creates. In an ideal situation this interface is a simple isolated thing in your application.

If you just let it do its thing, expect a monolith. You shouldn't rely on it coming up with interfaces that mesh well with what you had in mind, and each of those interfaces represents a decision that it took, restricting future iterations of the code. So a monolith is not only what you can expect, but also the best you can hope for.

If you want to let it cook, create more places for code that does a thing and you don't care how.

children.text: We use cost per pass, not average cost per task, because we want to see the harness keep a high pass rate and low cost at the same time.

In this case, I am not entirely sure how cost per pass is distinct from cost per successful task given that success is defined as pass/fail.

To illustrate the difference, the author of FrontierHarness included "Figure 3. Cost and pass rate of each harness with each model", in which we can see that Codex CLI has $0.937 cost per pass, but a $0.573 cost per task. Measuring cost per task also changes the winner to OpenCode

"Cost per pass" is distinct from "cost per successful task."

Cost per pass is simply the average cost per task divided by the pass rate.

If you draw a line from the origin to any harness on that chart, its slope (pass rate ÷ cost) represents passes per dollar. Cost per pass is the inverse of that slope, meaning the lowest cost per pass gives you the steepest line.

These are cool results and I'm glad that tokens are being invested to eval harness capabilities.

However, I am hesitant on the correlation between pass/fail in evals which are a binary 0/1 determined by tests, and real world usage, where users can steer, run code review, and care about more than just test pass/fail.

I wrote about the problem of determining "success" for coding agents, and a lot of it boils down to the fact that agents can write dumb code that passes tests, and write smart code that fails tests, and we need to shift to rewarding quality of code and alignment with intent rather than just signal on held out tests (which is still important!)

I don't like this framing.

For a given model, the best harness depends on the problem. As models become increasingly capable, the harness appears to matter more than the model. This is perhaps controversial but allow me to explain.

Most of my problems are in a single domain, using specific tools and programming languages. I give whatever model de jour the specific tools it needs to solve the problem. I don't let it execute arbitrary scripts or programs (though it can, if it really tries). I give it a restricted number of calls and I feed that information back into it (budget). I let it farm out work to other models, using the same harness. I give everything a budget, which is tracked and enforced, but it's not real, and refills at different times.

This bespoke, specialized harness absolutely smokes any other mainstream harness for these tasks. Significantly faster, cheaper, more correct.

But I can't build a mobile app with this harness, or make a movie.

These tests are doing the same thing. They measure a handful of scenarios. I can't easily tell if those map to my needs or not. In my experience, very few of them do.

Can these general purpose harnesses solve my problems? Yes, if I'm willing to let the model churn for a long time and burn a lot of tokens. But that doesn't feel like a sustainable practice.

Maybe I'm too early, maybe it's premature to optimize the harness this way, but I'm spending fewer tokens than my peers and getting a lot more done, and that matters.

children.author: krawczstef
children.text:
There's no IP in a harness, and they don't matter that much.

Harnesses simply make different choices around certain context engineering things, what they name tools, how they compact, their system prompt, etc.

So it's not surprising that they work "better" for some models than others, but I'd bet that if you made each harness have same system prompt and tool names, the variance would shrink further...

So I would say know what you're optimizing for and construct the harness you need for it instead (it's just a while loop with an llm call and function calling after all) ...
